Mr. Chairman, I was pointing out that there are several sources from which much of the criticism could emanate. The third group to which I was referring is composed of those sincere individuals who are frustrated in their attempts to gain an understanding of the issues involved, and who therefore accept whatever is said in the public press, or whatever is passed along to them. In view of the fact that there is nothing to present the other side of the picture to them, they accept the story they hear or read, when actually it may be far from the truth.
I think a very significant statement was made by Mr. Erwin D. Canham, of London, in the Christian Science Monitor of Thursday, May 27, 1965, when he said:
The Viet Nam crisis and now the Dominican crisis furnish very convenient sticks with which to beat the United States in the Central European Communist countries.
He went on to say:
It suits the Communists, naturally, to make the United States the villain of world politics. As a great power with heavy and awkward duties, the United States bear a burden of unpopularity with many non-Communist nations as well.
A true and growing detente does not seem to me to be the actual goal of Soviet policies. The isolation and lessening of American power is. Therefore if the Soviets had not been presented with the gratuitous issues of Viet Nam, Santo Domingo, and the Johnson attitudes as compared with the Kennedy style, they would seek other methods of stirring up resentments.
I realize my time is limited and a great number of areas of world interest have been referred to in this debate, but there are two which seem to be of prime concern at the moment, Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic. So far as Viet Nam is concerned I do not know just who knows all the facts, if anybody does, but we are aware that violence has plagued this unhappy country for many years, and the question of concern is whether Western policy is that desired by the people of South Viet Nam, or is it designed to perpetuate a regime which the people do not want? This is something which was referred to by the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam.
I am not going to take the time to recount again the history of South Viet Nam, but

May 28. 1965
Supply-External Affairs the Secretary of State for External Affairs has stated the reasons for the development of this critical problem-the expansionist tactics of Communism, infiltration and subversion-and there are others that have not been mentioned. I appreciate the fact that both he and the Government recognize that military solution of itself will not be sufficient. It must go beyond that.
I think there is a tendency to rely too much upon the military aspects of our efforts to contain Communism. It may be that these are necessary to give an opportunity for the working of other influences and factors, but in this particular case I believe that there should be the fullest possible pursuit, through negotiation, of a satisfactory solution to the problem. We all know the dangers. We recognize the fact that escalation of the war in that area could engulf not only Asia but the whole world. I am convinced that the military operations may be justified and are necessary to an extent, but I am even more convinced that there must be negotiations on every conceivable level, at every possible time, in order to effect a satisfactory solution.
I have here a clipping from the Christian Science Monitor of March 1, 1965, which quotes Senator Wayne Morse of Oregon, as follows:
I am calling for an international conference with non-combatants sitting at the head of the table, and the combatants on the two sides, to try to see what we can do to set up a rule of law in Asia-honourable in its implementation to both sides-under which the third-party force, through the United Nations, would maintain the peace in Asia until the happy day comes when the combatants can lay down their arms, and there will be war no more.
I believe this is essential if we are going to have a satisfactory solution to the problems in this area.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the fact that President Johnson had offered to negotiate unconditionally. The hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam says that is not true. Perhaps there is room for debate even on an issue like that, but nevertheless we believe negotiation is of the highest importance and must be pursued on every possible occasion. .
I trust that the Government and the Secretary of State for External Affairs are bending every effort to find a meeting ground, some place and at some level, where those who are concerned can get together and negotiate to try and settle this tragic situation. So far as the policy of the United States is concerned, it may be open to question. Indeed
tMr. Patterson.]
it is open to question, but I do know the SEATO organization has supported it and that Australia and New Zealand are sending at least token forces to indicate their full support of the U.S. operations.
[DOT] (5:10 p.m.)
I trust that out of this there will evolve a plan whereby peace can be restored and the Vietnamese people themselves can decide their own future and work out their own destiny, in a way that will be satisfactory to them and conducive to world peace. Canada, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs says, has no obligation or commitment in this area other than as a Member of the supervisory team. But what concerns Canada today is this: Though we may have no commitment at the present time, in the event of an escalation of the conflict we should find ourselves involved whether we want to be involved or not. This is why we are so concerned about it.
The Dominican Republic has been referred to as another area of grave and immediate concern. This was a situation which developed when it was feared there would be a repetition of the Cuban situation. The United States Government moved in and acted as a buffer between the two opposing forces. Of course, in doing so it brought itself under serious and concentrated criticism. The United States authorities apparently saw a new Cuba in the making. Whether this fear was real or not, we are not in a position to judge at the moment; only time may reveal just what is behind this whole unhappy situation, whether it was a popular revolt or whether it was a Communist inspired plot. The fact remains that the country was plunged into a civil war. We can at least say that by moving in the United States saved many lives and gave time for reflection on both sides. The enforced pause in the conflict will, it is hoped, lead to a political settlement satisfactory to all concerned. We know that with the entry of a force under the O.A.S. and in harmony with the United Nations the United States has withdrawn some of its forces and is continuing to do so. Here again it seems to me that a lot of loose and irresponsible sniping has taken place at the expense of those concerned in this critical situation, attacks which have done more harm than good, and which has contributed to the agitation of this problem rather than to its diminution.
I am not sure how much time I have left. But coming back to the United Nations I
May 28, 1965
should like to think of the responsibility of that organization. I think it has been set out clearly by the President of the Assembly. He stated it as follows: the maintenance of peace, the elimination of colonialism and the improvement of economic and social conditions in underdeveloped nations. As far as Canada's responsibility in the world is concerned, we sometimes like to think of ourselves as being, perhaps, bigger than we are. At other times it may be we think of ourselves as being smaller than we really are. But I believe Canada has an important part to play in the international field and one of our main objects should be to project an image of this country which would show the world what can be done under a system of free competitive enterprise when the evils of capitalism, as some people refer to them, have been eliminated and where a system which has been approved and supported through the generations can work to the advantage of people as a whole and bring happiness and security, not only to ourselves but to all the nations round about. This is one of the main contributions Canada can make.
Another is in the field of peace keeping and mediation. We are fulfilling our responsibility in the field of peace keping operations. Again I exhort the Secretary of State for External Affairs, if he needs exhortation, to move forward with resolution and courage in this field and do everything humanly possible to bring about an understanding of each other's problems, so that the nations may consider each other's views and live in harmony to the advantage of all.
Finally I am of the opinion that Canada could do far more through the medium of foreign aid, both material and technical, to erase some of the circumstances and conditions which are conducive to revolt and to the spread of Communism. People who enjoy the necessities of life and are able to lead contented lives with a measure of security will not be too interested in the revolutionary type of operation offered to them as the only means of achieving economic liberty and freedom.
In conclusion may I say this: The United States is carrying a tremendous responsibility as the leading nation in the Western alliance in the defence of the free world. It is possible the United States will make mistakes. It is possible their foreign policy will not be correct on every occasion. Nevertheless
Supply-External Affairs I think we ought to consider the position of that country as a leader in the defence of freedom. Instead of sniping and fussing, we ought to consider her responsibility and make our contribution as best we can to the development and promotion of peace and good will among the peoples of the world.

As a relatively new Member contributing to this debate I consider myself somewhat as a buck private in an army of generals. Nevertheless, as a buck private in the last rank of the last company in the battalion, though I may not be able to tell how the parade looks I can see whether the general's stars are straight and whether his medals are well pinned on.
I take part in the debate today as one who has had no close acquaintance with the negotiations which have been going on in connection with these world crises. I have heard the Leader of the Opposition speak. I have listened to the Secretary of State for External Affairs, the hon. Member for Burnaby-Co-quitlam and the hon. Member for Fraser Valley. I know that some of these hon. Members have been very active in the external affairs of this country and in world affairs generally. The Leader of the Opposition has, of course, taken a leading part in these affairs, as Prime Minister of this country, and the Secretary of State for External Affairs is now in the midst of this turmoil. The hon. Member for Bumaby-Coquitlam was the premier of a province for a number of years. I trust their judgment on my comments will not be too severe and that I may be able to contribute to some extent to clarifying this present situation. If I adopt the attitude I intend to adopt it is because the eminent people who have just spoken have found themselves in the midst of all this turmoil.
[DOT] (5:20 p.m.)
Sometimes, when you are in a turmoil it is pretty difficult to find a way out. This is the time when sometimes somebody from the outside can help you get out. Before you can get out of a turmoil like that, it is always good to find out how you got into it in the first place. I sometimes wonder if we actually know how we got into all this mess and why the quarrels that occur so often across the globe are repeated again and again.
The hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam referred to "this ever shrinking world". It is a fact that the world seems to be shrinking because of these errors we are walking into. Sometimes the errors are caused by haste,



May 28, 1965
Supply-External Affairs and sometimes by the incomprehension that exists with regard to various problems. They are caused by everybody going in every direction and not knowing exactly where they are going or why. There is no light of any kind to guide them; but they are right in the middle of the turmoil and are trying to do the best with what they have.
I believe that with regard to our external affairs problems we should be guided by our inner conscience, first of all. We should consider external affairs as we consider our internal affairs, because they are no different from what we have to undergo in our own country. It is a fact that today these difficulties come upon countries very rapidly, and the more we advance in time, the faster they come, the more numerous and complicated they seem to get. Why do we have all these complications? Maybe, Mr. Chairman, it is because in different parts of the world there are some who wish to hang on to things and will not let go. This maintains a high-tension wire across the world.
We have the Viet Nam crisis at the moment; we have the crisis in the Dominican Republic, not to mention all the other turmoil that has been happening in the past few years. Then there is the tension that is building up in other parts of the world at the present time. We hear doubts about the future if we maintain the positions that have been taken so far. Are the situations in the Viet Nam crisis and in Santo Domingo new? Is this the first time we have had to face such problems? I should say not, Mr. Chairman; this is not the first time we have had to face them-they have been repeated again and again throughout history. I think that to find out why these things have happened we have to look back at history, and find out exactly where we left off and what were the reasons that drove us to this point. You can be sure there has always been a cause for this sort of trouble. They were probably caused in the first place by somebody who did not mind his own business; that is usually one of the causes. More trouble is started by somebody not minding his own business than when people do mind their own business. But who did not mind his own business in this situation? Who is the cause of the present troubles?
If we go back through history, I think this situation has been repeated throughout. I do not want to be a moral historian, but one can at least be a practical historian; and sometimes when we are a little more prac-
[Mr. Langlois.l
tical, use a little more common sense and less political sense, we obtain better results and at a faster rate.
If we look back on history we see it has not been only military forces that have ruled. This is not something new. Before all this trouble started, if you look back on history you find that people ruled in the past on the basis of superstition. We had this situation in Canada before the white man ever came here; there were medicine men in this country that ruled their tribes on superstition, and the whole of this country was ruled in that way. You can go back to the time of the high priests and the Inquisition; they ruled at that time on the basis of the principles and beliefs of superstition. This has been largely overcome, although we still have traces of it in our modern civilization. This business of superstition is not so strong now, but we still have it.
This was overcome throughout the years by the force of the sword, the rule of the sword. This form of rule came into power next, and if we look back through the Middle Ages and at the Roman Empire we find that the sword was the rule-the stronger the nation, the better off it was. The country that had the biggest army and was the richest ruled the land. I am not saying it is different today. After revolutions and turmoil we still have people in this world who do not want to be ruled by the sword of the almighty king. Louis XIV of France said, "The state is I. It is the law because I wish it so". That was pretty drastic at that time, but it was the way the country was ruled. What the king wanted, he got; what the people wanted did not matter.
We overcame the rule of the sword with what is now a race to the cash box. This is the force that prevails today; it is the force that is having the greatest effect on the affairs of the world. You can be sure of that, Mr. Chairman. If it were not for some financial interest somewhere in the world we would not have half the trouble that we now have. This is one of the reasons for all this mess in the world today. Revolutions have occurred in countries where hunger prevails; revolutions have occurred in countries perhaps because of unscrupulous exploiters of some natural resources. We have seen a revolution in Cuba and there have been revolutions in other countries. And we will be seeing revolutions in Latin America before too long, if we do not change our outlook on how to solve these problems which face us today.

The world situation at the present time is caused by a conflict between those trying to exploit and those trying to make an honest living, but who are living in hunger and misery. We have come out of this turmoil and this blackness across the globe with two main ideas, and I must say that they are forming within regions and within blocs fairly rapidly. We have the idea of state control and Communism in the Eastern bloc, on the one hand, and we have the democratic way of life on the other hand. There are still points that we have to learn in our own democratic way of life. We see our southern neighbours trying to uproot our democracy by their methods. They do not always approve of the way of life in some other country, and tell the other people what to do; but they themselves have a lot to learn with regard to their own democratic way of life, when one considers the racial discriminations that are found to exist in that country. One has to look back not later than two or three weeks ago to the situation that existed with regard to the Ku Klux Klan, and the trial that took place in that country.
[DOT] (5:30 p.m.)
If lawyers in the United States take the stand which this lawyer took not more than two or three weeks ago, we still have a long way to go toward civilization.
I wonder how Washington has the nerve to intervene in one manner or another in the present quarrels across the globe. Many times we find foreign interests at the bottom of these conflicts. I said that there were two blocs, the Democratic bloc and the Communist bloc. These two main ideals will be facing each other before too long. Even within one government one finds different conceptions, some to the right and some to the left. If we solve our problems with guns and bombs, which country today would not be at war? If we And peace within our own boundaries here, it is because we have an institution within which we can work together without using force of any kind. If this institution of parliament today has been built up over the years into its present image, it is because it has some good in it. We must find ways of bringing these two blocs together, one side or the other giving up. Everyone seems to try to maintain to a certain extent the democratic way of life, and we in the Western bloc can be proud of ours. But we must also defend it and help others who wish to acquire it. To do this we must find out, first of all, what these people need.
Supply-External Affairs
Even though we have the United Nations, NATO, NORAD and other world organizations, if we do not find out what these nations need then how can we give them what they want? Practically two thirds of the world's people today go to bed at night hungry. Therefore we must be neighbours and allies to these people, not aggressors. This has not always been our line of action. Even our southern neighbour has sometimes taken advantage in this respect. They have helped some nations under the flag of help, but sometimes we have noticed they did not always do what they should. Some European nations have done the same thing. They have professed to help underdeveloped nations, and the first thing one knows is a revolution occurs because they are exploited to the bone. This sort of thing we must prevent. Practically every Communist country in the world today turns to Communism because its people are hungry, and possibly because they were offered something we did not offer, namely food, shelter, and to a certain extent security. I am not referring to freedom and individual liberty of the people in the Eastern bloc, but wherever hunger prevails there remains the need for food.
I think the Secretary of State for External Affairs should defend this approach today. He should find out what these people need. I am sure not one of them wants war. Not one of them wants United States troops in Viet Nam or in Santo Domingo. All of them want peace. All of them strive for individual peace and quiet. They all want security.
Canada might be a small country in the matter of warfare. But is this how we measure the strength of a nation-by the number of planes, bombs and missiles it possesses? No, Sir, you do not. You measure the strength of a nation by its good will, by its internal wealth and what it can do for other nations and for its own people. That is how you measure the strength of a nation and its government. This is where the Secretary of State for External Affairs should guide the thinking of his colleagues, his other Ministers, who are involved in this international turmoil. We have replaced the sword, but by what? By bombs? They are not much better; in fact they are worse. We have already had two world wars. If things maintain their present trend-this will be verified in a few years' time; and I am not the only one who has come to this conclusion because some university historians have also reached the same conclusion-then I make this prediction. We are

May 28, 1965
Supply-External Affairs going into the third world war now between the United States of America and Russia. I am referring to the cold war, and its little fireflies flying around, with sparks here and there, but no main fire. But as I have said, where there is hunger and misery there will be revolution and war. The next war will not be between the United States and Russia; I am pretty sure of that. The next war will be between Mainland China and the U.S.S.R.
Why do I say that? First of all, there is poverty today in China. It has overpopulated areas. It cannot contain its present population. It could move toward India but that is not the natural debouche, the natural way out. The natural and logical way out will be to the north, toward Siberia. I visualize one mighty government in Russia and another in Mainland China. When that situation develops, which one will be chosen?-and I should like to know about that choice if it has to be made in five or eight years time.
[DOT] (5:40 p.m.)
We must recognize that the situations exist before the clashes commence. Today the world is engaged in a race to see who puts the first man on the moon, and which country can develop the greater number of atomic weapons. Good Lord, Sir, we could now blow this world up, and the flash of the explosion would not even be visible on the nearest planet; so why should we worry about making a flash in this sense.
Surely our job is to go out and help those nations that need assistance, and this can be done through the Department of External Affairs. During the war we were not a large country as far as the world picture was concerned, but surely we are big enough that we can help to feed those people of the world who are starving. I am sure we would accomplish a great deal more in this manner than will be accomplished through an attempt to be water boys of the United States team.
I should not like people to think that I am anti-United States. They must accept the responsibility for their own actions; but if we believe that they are wrong in their policies, it is up to us to try to get them to change their minds. Surely if we believe that we are right, we should stand up and defend our ideas. I do not believe that we can solve the problems of the world today by force. Surely force is not the solution to the problems which exist today in Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic, or in other areas where conflict is taking place. While it might be necessary to support peace keeping operations such as that which has taken place on Cyprus,

I think we can obtain our goals more expeditiously by providing a lead in assisting underdeveloped nations. I am sure that we can achieve our desires in a much more effective way by helping the underdeveloped and underfed countries of the world.
Most of the difficulties now facing the world are direct results of conflicts of interest. Very often these differences develop into expanding turmoils and it is up to us to prevent them by initiating negotiations between the conflicting countries. We should provide a lead in co-ordinating efforts directed toward the maintenance of peace, security and freedom.
I should like to conclude by reading from a communique I have just received from the Voice of Women, and I hope the words of this organization will be considered seriously by the Minister. Submissions made by this organization have received serious consideration in the past and I think at this time, in view of the circumstances with which we are now faced, this expression is even more valuable than any received before.

The Voice of Women, sharing fully the feelings of urgency which led the government to hold a debate on this country's foreign policy, has decided to interrupt its annual convention now taking place at Carleton University to send a delegation authorized to meet the leaders of the various political parties.
The Voice of Women states that any war may now lead the world to catastrophe and we assert once again that conflicts of interests can no longer be settled by the use of force.
Therefore, we ask the representatives of the Canadian people to state that we are a nation that wishes to remain an instrument of world peace. They must then openly express our disapproval of the American intervention in South Viet Nam and the Dominican Republic, an intervention which constitutes a glaring violation of the principle of self-determination for all peoples as set out in the United Nation's charter.
Well spoken.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity, that presents itself in the discussion of the main estimates of the Department of External Affairs, to draw to the attention of the House a question which is of paramount importance to the nation. This is an international matter, governed by an international treaty, and properly comes within the purview of the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I refer to the question in respect of the water levels of Lake Ontario and the St. Lawrence River in particular, although some of my references may be directed to the Great Lakes as a whole.
May 28, 1965

The reason I wish to speak at this time, and I am happy to do so, relates to the fact that this is the month of May when the greatest flood waters are moving down the rivers, through the lakes, toward the sea, and if action is delayed in impounding those waters for the benefit of this country as a whole we will lose another year, because we will have to wait for the melting snows and spring run-offs in 1966, should we have another drought this year similar to those we experienced in 1964 and 1963.
This question is highlighted today by a strong and forthright editorial which appeared in the Montreal Gazette this morning under the heading "Low Water Again". I am certain many of you will be amazed to learn that in April-last month-of this year the water level of the harbour of Montreal reached its lowest recorded point in history. As a Member for a Toronto riding, I should like to point out that in February of this year the water level in the Toronto harbour came within one quarter of an inch of its lowest recorded level in history. The lowest level in recorded history was reached in December of 1934, and in February, 1965, the level was within one quarter of an inch of that lowest level.
With Montreal now complaining about the low water level in the Montreal harbour, and with the residents of Toronto and of the Lake Ontario basin complaining of the low water level of Lake Ontario, I say, as a Member from the Toronto area, which is vitally affected by this situation, that the Department of External Affairs should give immediate attention to the operations of the International Joint Commission. The International Joint Commission is a joint body of the United States and Canada, but it falls within the purview of the Secretary of State for the United States and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for Canada, and I suggest that it is not doing its duty.
The water of the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River is controlled by an international treaty signed in 1909 by Lord Bryce of Great Britain on behalf of Canada and by Elihu Root on behalf of the United States. In article VIII of that treaty covering boundary waters of the Great Lakes there is listed a table of precedence relating to the value of the water. I should like to read part of this article, as follows:
The High Contracting Parties-
That is Great Britain on behalf of Canada, and the United States.
Supply-External Affairs
-shall have, each on its own side of the boundary, equal and similar rights in the use of the waters hereinbefore defined as boundary waters.
The following order of precedence shall be observed among the various uses enumerated hereinafter for these waters, and no use shall be permitted which tends materially to conflict with or restrain any other use which is given preference over it in this order of precedence:
(1)	Uses for domestic and sanitary purposes:
(2)	Uses for navigation, including the service of canals for the purposes of navigation:
(3)	Uses for power and for irrigation purposes.
This problem is highlighted today by the interesting fact that the people living in the basin of Lake Ontario are demanding that this treaty be enforced by the two Governments and that priority No. 1 be observed. The water level of Lake Ontario today is 17 inches below the average level for the past 105 years, and this is adversely affecting domestic and sanitary purposes, which is the first item in this table of precedence. We in the Lake Ontario basin are determined that the treaty shall be enforced and the table of precedence observed so that the people on the shores of the lake will enjoy priority No. 1. But we have the City of Montreal through its voice, the Montreal Gazette, asking today that priority No. 2 be observed and in that regard the Gazette argues, and argues correctly, that the power interests of this continent are being allowed in practice to wreck the table of precedence completely, and are getting a priority they do not enjoy by international agreement. The Montreal Gazette points out that the trouble in Montreal harbour has come about because priority is being given to requests for the provision of water for the generating of hydroelectric power. They also point out that in the table of precedence for the use of boundary v/aters, power and irrigation come at the end of the list.
[DOT] (5:50 p.m.)
I would ask hon. Members to note the Montreal Gazette's statement that at the end of the list comes use for power and irrigation. There are three items only in that table of precedence, and at the end of the list comes power and irrigation. But I have in my hand a copy of a speech delivered in the Ontario Legislature by the spokesman for the Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission. The Ontario Hydro-Electric Power Commission is one of three power entities that make use of the water flowing down the St. Lawrence for power purposes, the other two being the New York State Power Authority and the Quebec Hydro-Electric

May 28, 1965
Supply-External Affairs Power Commission. There are three power organizations interested in developing power on the St. Lawrence.
What does this speech of the spokesman for Ontario Hydro, delivered in the Ontario Legislature on February 3 of this year, say? The Montreal Gazette points out that the low water level in Montreal harbour is due to the fact that priority is being given to power purposes, and the Gazette emphasizes that power is at the end of the list. But here we have the spokesman for the Ontario Hydro pointing out something that I think is amazing:
In the precedence for users of the lakes established in the 1909 treaty, power production is high on the list, In third place, after domestic water supplies and navigation.
Here you have a spokesman for the power interests talking about the last item on the list being in a high position. Montreal demands that the treaty be enforced and that the second position in the table of precedence, navigation, which would help Montreal harbour, be observed over and against the third item in the table of precedence, power and irrigation.
As a Member from Toronto and one who represents voters residing on the shores of Lake Ontario I demand that the first item in the table of precedence be observed. We know that those responsible for Toronto harbour are dissatisfied with the present arrangement, just the same as those responsible for Montreal harbour. I spoke in the House on May 11 and pointed out that the problem with regard to Lake Ontario and Toronto harbour could be solved if the International Joint Commission would close the dam at Iroquois. If they will close the dam at Iroquois they can hold Lake Ontario at any predetermined level. While the flood waters are rushing down to the sea, I would ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to take steps immediately to see that the International Joint Commission closes the dam gates at Iroquois in order that the level of water can be raised 17 inches to the 105 year average and to see that the level is held there. I do not want to see the level brought up to the average figure for 105 years, and then water released for power development purposes later, resulting in establishing a new low level.
I say that Quebec demands that item No. 2 in the table of precedence, navigation, be observed over and above item No. 3 which has to do with power. On the other hand, Ontario demands that item No. 1 in the table

of precedence be observed. I say that the Department of External Affairs should give immediate attention to the enforcement of this treaty which has been in effect since 1909, and is still of vital force as an international agreement. If we cannot observe treaties that affect us within 60 miles of Ottawa and the Parliament buildings, why ask us to observe international treaties that apply half way around the world? Let us see to it that we observe international treaties affecting us at home before we start to go tens of thousands of miles away to enforce treaties that are not as vital to us as the International Boundary Waters Treaty of 1909.

Mr. Chairman, I hope there are a few minutes left so that I may say a few words. I was much impressed by the speech of the hon. Member for Burnaby-Coquitlam. I did not agree with everything he said, but I do agree with him that it is time we took a stand and spoke strongly and distinctly. When we are considering international affairs and what action the Government should take we have got to remember what we are standing for. Are we just fighting against Communism, without caring what the results are so long as we are fighting Communism? Are we prepared to say that the rights of other peoples do not mean anything and that we are willing to use anybody on any occasion and abuse them in any way we like in the struggle against Communism? I think this is something v/e have to take a look at right now if we are going to consider what attitude the Government should take toward the action now being taken by that leader of the Western world, the United States.
To begin with, the situation in Viet Nam has excited more than a few of us. Certainly we are not suggesting that the situation there is a simple one and that solutions are easy. But there have been a couple of things in the action of the Americans there that must surely give us all pause. In the first place, one American spokesman summed up the dilemma of the United States in Viet Nam when he said that the main trouble there is that the people of South Viet Nam will not help themselves. That was an official American spokesman, the Secretary of Defence, I believe, and he was giving the official American view with regard to the difficulty in South Viet Nam. He said that the people there would not help themselves. What he was really saying was that they were not going to help the Americans. If the Ameri-
May 28, 19SS

cans are not in that country to help the people there, what the devil are they doing there and how can their actions be justified?
Certainly the situation in the Dominican Republic is even plainer. There is no suggestion of intervention at anyone's request. This is not a case of the United States moving in to protect their own nationals. I doubt that they would have the right to do that in any event in the circumstances, but I will not argue that point now. However, there is no doubt from the action they took that they moved in for the purpose of making sure that no government could take power there unless it met with the approval of the United States. It was as simple as that.
I suggest to members of the committee that if we start to think about why we want to stop Communism and why Communism has been the big bogeyman of international affairs for so many years, it is simply because we say that the international Communists would insist on their right to move into a country and would deny the people of that country the right of self-determination, in that by the use of power they would force those people to accept a government acceptable to the Communists. Is that not why people are afraid of the Communists? Is that not why we have always criticized them? But now, in the name of stopping this bogeyman, the United States is apparently doing exactly the same thing.
I suggest that the people of the Dominican Republic or the people of South Viet Nam are not really too concerned about what kind of dictator they get. Whether he calls himself an American or a Communist, he is a dictator and I am sure they want to get rid of him. We owe more than lip service to the principle of self-determination.
I see it is six o'clock, Mr. Chairman. I wish I had a little more time to develop that theme but perhaps I will be able to do so *at some other time.
Progress reported.
